segments_en: One does not recite Mizmor LeSodah on Shabbos or Yom Tov. Nine additional Tehillim are added here. One should not recite HaShamayim Mesaprim on weekdays. This also appears from the words of the Zohar. See Beit Yosef, siman 50.

On the eve of Yom Kippur one does not recite Mizmor LeSodah. Some say that it is likewise omitted on the eve of Tisha B'Av and on Tisha B'Av itself. See Hagahos Minhagim, Hilchos Tisha B'Av, seif 5. Others say that this is an error. Were the Beis HaMikdash rebuilt, offerings would be brought and Tisha B'Av would become a day of joy and celebration, and there would then be no fast. This is stated by Maharshal in responsum 4.

segments_en: If some of the congregation leave after the chazzan has begun the repetition aloud and Kedushah, those who remain may complete the entire order of Kedushah, including U'va LeTzion and the Kaddish that follows it.

The same principle applies to Maariv. If they began Vehu Rachum with ten and some then left, they complete the service through Yir'u Eineinu and also recite the Kaddish that follows, because that Kaddish belongs to Shema and its blessings. They may then recite the silent Maariv Shemoneh Esrei, since ten are not required for the silent prayer. The Kaddish following Shemoneh Esrei, however, may be recited only when ten are present. Similarly, even if Aleinu was begun with ten and some then left, the Mourner's Kaddish that follows may not be recited with fewer than ten. If Aleinu was recited without ten, the Kaddish afterward may not later be recited even after ten arrive. The same applies to Tehillim and Shir HaYichud. If they were completed without ten, the Kaddish afterward may not be recited even if ten are now present. Conversely, if ten were present during Tehillim or Shir HaYichud but were no longer present when the time for Kaddish arrived, the Kaddish is not recited. This is the accepted practice, as stated by Lechem Chamudos. I have likewise seen the practice in some places that when Tehillim is being recited without ten, they leave one chapter of Tehillim to be recited after ten arrive. The reason appears to be that this Kaddish, being of rabbinic institution, does not possess sufficient force to be recited merely because ten were present earlier, nor does the reverse case permit it.

segments_en: The Jew is liable when he tells the non-Jew,

Even if he later deposited it with another non-Jew, etc. This is from Hagahos Alfasi at the beginning of Pesachim. It appears obvious that if the non-Jew originally placed his chametz in another non-Jew's domain and the Jew accepted liability for it there, the Jew need not remove it. Beit Yosef writes that if the Jew designated a corner for the non-Jew, he need not remove it, so this case is certainly no more stringent, since the chametz was placed in the non-Jew's domain from the outset, even though the Jew accepted liability. Many proofs may be brought for this. If the Jew bears no liability, he is not obligated to remove it, but he must place before it a partition ten tefachim high. Even when a specific place was designated for the non-Jew, one should be stringent and require a partition ten tefachim high. Maharitz writes as follows: With due respect to his Torah scholarship, it appears to me that no proof can be brought from that case. There, the owner of the chametz is a Jew. Therefore, there is also a concern in the opposite direction. If the robber does not tell the owner,

segments_en: If they stipulated, etc. Rambam; and as written there,

(Likkut) If they stipulated, etc. There is another approach according to the Semag; see the Beit Yosef. The Kesef Mishnah explains the Rambam's reasoning: with profit, the managing partner receives an additional one-third from the deposit portion, because that additional amount is received as compensation for his labor with the deposit portion. Therefore he receives it from the deposit portion, whether large or small, according to the size of the deposit portion. This is unlike a loss, where he receives nothing as profit. Rather, as compensation for his labor, an amount is deducted from his loss so that he does not lose as much. The deduction is calculated according to the recipient's loss in his own portion, and one-third of his loss is deducted, so that he never loses more than two-thirds of the recipient's portion. See the Beit Yosef, who cites those who explain the case of half the profit and one-third, etc., not as requiring that he have one-sixth more in profit than in loss, but merely some small amount. See there, where he explains the words of the Rif and the Rosh in accordance with the Rambam and the Tur. His words do not appear correct. End.
